lead: Rapid City never forgets the 1972 flood. Today, hail, deep cold and flash floods off the Black Hills cause most of the water damage people call about.
risk: flash flooding, hail damage and frozen pipes
why: On June 9, 1972, heavy rain over the Black Hills sent Rapid Creek through the middle of the city. The flood killed 238 people and destroyed more than 1,300 homes. Afterward, Rapid City turned much of the floodplain into parks and open space, which is why a long greenway now follows the creek. Flash floods still happen in nearby canyons when summer storms stall over the hills.

Hail is the most common cause of claims. Storms roll off the hills almost every summer and crack shingles, siding and windows. Winters bring sharp cold, and pipes freeze in crawl spaces and outside walls. About 5% of Rapid City homes are mobile or manufactured homes. Their plumbing runs under the floor, where it freezes more easily and leaks can go unseen.
image_alt: Roofer kneeling on a roof with tools
image_caption: Hail is the most common cause of roof claims in Rapid City.
problems: Low areas near Rapid Creek and canyons
Older homes in North Rapid, West Boulevard
tips: Get a roof check after any hailstorm, even with no leak yet.
Wrap pipes and skirt mobile homes before the first hard freeze.
Know the flash flood risk if you live near a canyon or creek.
Keep gutters clear so melting snow drains away.
areas: Calls come from Downtown, West Boulevard, North Rapid, Robbinsdale, Canyon Lake and Sioux Park, plus Box Elder, Black Hawk and Summerset.

faq.q: Does my Rapid City home policy cover hail damage?
faq.a: Most home policies cover hail damage to the roof and siding, and the rain that gets in through it. Many South Dakota policies have a separate wind and hail deductible, often a percentage of your home's value. Check yours before storm season so a claim is not a surprise.
